Terminal output, JSON, inline GitHub comments, body findings and the ledger carry these diagnostics. Default rendering names the claim, reporting check and rule, judgement, reported severity, minimum and reason. A lowering also shows its target and reason, even on a non-speaking member. Render its reason once; omit the ordinary lowering line when the trust-floor note already carries it. When any minimum is acknowledge, show **Trust floor: acknowledge required; maintainer dismissal needed.** For lower minima, say that reported-severity policy requires no acknowledgement. Refutations also say **Verifier refuted this claim; maintainer review still required.** Each host escapes the text with its existing renderer.

The attack read 217 rounds from 78 stores. The phase-1 floor would have raised 12 distinct findings: two lowered and ten refuted. Two refuted trust P1s, `be0f7db9` and `1222cd57`, are valid in [the record for pull request #98](../../packages/evals/comparisons/2026-10-16-pr-98.md). Refutation therefore needs the floor too. F1 reduces the protected refutations needing acknowledgement from ten to five under the historical policies.

Choice: `melian dismiss <range|#pr> <id> --reason <text>` records the dismissal on the finding's lifecycle record in the changeset's local storage, with the git author as the dismisser, `git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT` without its timestamp, and the time. The reason is required, trimmed, and at most 1,000 characters. The same commit starts an adjudication over the review's own input, so the stored verdict counts the finding out at once and a later review of the revision attaches to that adjudication. Dismissing a dismissed finding replaces its reason and keeps the old dismissal in its history, as a reopened one does; the same dismisser giving the same reason again changes nothing. A finding adjudication merged from several checks' reports is dismissed whole, every report merged into it with it, and visibly: `review` and `findings` print each finding's merged reports with their severity, rule, check, and ID, `dismiss` names every report it dismissed with the finding by rule, check, and ID, and `--only` dismisses the report its ID names alone, leaving the other reports live. An ID names the finding with that exact ID first, and a dismissed report a live finding lists beside it never leads to that finding. A finding carries its dismissal and past dismissals, so `melian findings --all` and the JSON show who, when, and why. The terminal rendering ends each finding's first line with its ID.

If the maintainer wants this narrowed, write it as an `Amends:` of 2026-10-17-trust-floor-exact-rule. Give it a mechanical test a model cannot be talked out of, for example: the flagged lines are byte-identical to text already on the default branch, moved or re-wrapped. explanation.whyHere: The floor exists because verifier refutations of protected claims were wrong in practice. Two refuted trust P1s on pull request #98 were valid. Melian's own prompt text is the worst member of the class to exempt: every later review loads those prompts as instructions. An injection there is read first by the verifier, a model, and then by the coordinator, an agent, and either can be the target of the injected text. properties.failureScenario:
1. A builder's pull request edits `.melian/lenses/design/LENS.md`, or a prompt string in `packages/pipeline`, which is Melian's own instructions for reviewers. It adds a sentence that reads like rewording but tells later lenses to treat findings under some path as out of scope.

# What the coordinator may do for the maintainer

Status: ruled by the maintainer on 2026-11-28, in the coordinator's session. The coordinator listed the delegations below, which the maintainer had given one at a time since 2026-10-17, and asked whether to write them into the repository. He answered "yes".

Amends: [When Melian cannot run, the maintainer overrides one commit](2026-10-23-melian-review-outage-procedure.md), who may post the override on a pull request's head: the coordinator too, under the four conditions below

## Problem

The maintainer delegated some of his reads and dismissals to the coordinator, in the coordinator's session. Nothing in the repository said so. A builder cannot check a delegation it cannot read, and all three post under the maintainer's login.

Example: on [pull request #662](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/662), the round's only finding above advisory was a policy notice on one new learning in AGENTS.md. The coordinator read the change and recorded its read. The builder declined to queue on it, rightly, and the pull request waited for the maintainer to answer "read".

## Choice

The coordinator may do these, and nothing else, in the maintainer's place:

1. **Read a policy notice.** The coordinator may read a `policy-change-review` notice on a file whose change it has read, and record that read on the pull request. A builder may queue on that record as it would on the maintainer's.
2. **Dismiss an equivalent mutant**, with a one-line reason that says why no input can tell the mutant from the code.
3. **Dismiss a finding that restates a ruling**: one whose only objection is to a rule the maintainer has ruled on. The dismissal names the ruling's date and where it was given.
4. **Dismiss a refuted injection flag on Melian's own prompt text**: a `melian/injection-attempt` finding the verifier refuted, where the flagged text is Melian's own prompt or its instructions for reviewers, and the coordinator has read the diff of that text and its meaning is unchang [cut at 2 KiB]

message.text: Delegation 5 lets the coordinator use the outage override for a whole class of heads: any head whose finished round raised nothing above advisory except policy notices. That class includes *blocking* `policy-change-review` notices on workflow and configuration files. Those notices set `melian/review` to `failure`, and at base they need a stored dismissal or a fix. The outage procedure was built for one case: Melian cannot run. Condition 1 requires that Melian did run and finished. So the override no longer stands in for a missing review. It overrules a review that ran and blocked.

evidence.snippet: Amends: [When Melian cannot run, the maintainer overrides one commit](2026-10-23-melian-review-outage-procedure.md), who may post the override on a pull request's head: the coordinator too, under the four conditions below

An unresolved finding that adjudication resolves `acknowledge` now fails `melian/review`, as a block does.
A maintainer dismisses it by ID, with a reason, and publishes again.
The lifecycle carries that dismissal across revisions until its trigger changes.
Reading a notice or replying on GitHub does not dismiss it.

Policy notices have no exemption. An undismissed notice that resolves `block` or `acknowledge` fails.
Every notice at those resolutions needs a stored dismissal, including notices on policy, standards and analyser configuration.
The maintainer accepts that work. The coordinator's former policy-notice exception cannot clear the required status.

Choice: `melian/review` is the only required context in a second ruleset with no bypass actors. When Melian cannot run, the maintainer posts a `melian/review` `success` on the chosen pull request's head. The merge-group job copies it to the group commit, and the pull request lands through the queue. The ruleset stays `active`. If the merge-group workflow itself cannot run, the maintainer posts the same override on the entry's group commit as well. Nothing disables the ruleset.

An acknowledge finding does not fail this status, by the maintainer's ruling. The builder asks the maintainer in its own session to read the finding, records the maintainer's read on the pull request, then marks it ready and queues it. `melian publish` keeps the amended decision's rule: an unresolved acknowledgement fails the status it sets. So an Actions status is a separate publisher class from a host publication until [issue #305](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/305) gives builders an identity of their own: its `success` records a maintainer's read, held on the pull request, rather than a dismissal held in a store.

The builder, not the coordinator, now marks its pull request ready and queues it, by the same ruling. The coordinator still runs the host round a dismissal or the comparison record needs. The maintainer's read of acknowledge findings is the independent step before the queue, and a blocking finding still needs a fix or a dismissal through a host round.

An acknowledge finding does not fail the status an Actions round sets, as [the decision](docs/decisions/2026-11-07-actions-round-sets-melian-review.md) records. So a pull request needs no host round when its `melian round` workflow run sets `melian/review` to `success` on the exact head, and the maintainer's read of each acknowledge finding is recorded on the pull request. Its builder marks it ready and queues it, from a cloud session through the REST routes in Working in a cloud session. A dismissal can be recorded only on the host, since an Actions round's store is thrown away. A policy notice prints as blocking on a workflow or configuration file and as acknowledge on AGENTS.md. A blocking one fails the status like any blocking finding, so it needs the host until a round can honour a dismissal; one at acknowledge needs the maintainer's read recorded, as above. This reading of the rule is the coordinator's. The maintainer agreed it on 2026-11-16, in the coordinator's session, with the ruling that builders finish clean pull requests themselves. [Pull request #499](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/499) landed this way.

Why: the root has no directory above it, so it was judged under its own settings, and a root that set `guardrails.policy-change-review.enabled: false` hid every later edit to itself. A pull request could then rewrite the repository's lens paths or guardrail rules with no maintainer asked to read the change. Judging the root under the built-in defaults alone closed that gap but opened another: a maintainer who raised the severity to `P1` so that policy edits block found an edit to the root itself only acknowledged at `P2`. A floor keeps both: no configuration file switches off or softens the review of itself, and a stricter choice still holds. The resolution needs the same floor: a root that maps `P2` to `silent` would otherwise pass a change to itself with no notice, though the guardrail reported it.

explanation.what: Delegation 5 lets the coordinator use the outage override for a whole class of heads: any head whose finished round raised nothing above advisory except policy notices. That class includes *blocking* `policy-change-review` notices on workflow and configuration files. Those notices set `melian/review` to `failure`, and at base they need a stored dismissal or a fix. The outage procedure was built for one case: Melian cannot run. Condition 1 requires that Melian did run and finished. So the override no longer stands in for a missing review. It overrules a review that ran and blocked.
explanation.whatToDo: Limit delegation 5 to the outage the procedure covers: no `melian round` could review the head. Exclude any head whose round raised a policy notice at `block`. Or, if the maintainer really wants the coordinator to clear blocking policy notices, add `Amends:` lines for 2026-10-17-acknowledge-status-exact-rule and 2026-11-07-actions-round-sets-melian-review, and give them a short attacking review, as the convergence rules require of a ruling that changes blocking behaviour. Either way, exclude any pull request the coordinator wrote itself.
explanation.whyHere: Several active base decisions rest on one assumption: a blocking policy notice, or one at acknowledge, is cleared only by the maintainer's stored dismissal. 2026-10-17-acknowledge-status-exact-rule says every notice at those resolutions needs a stored dismissal, and that "the coordinator's former policy-notice exception cannot clear the required status". 2026-11-07-actions-round-sets-melian-review says a blocking finding still needs a fix or a dismissal through a host round. The root-policy floor exists so that a policy edit never lands with "no maintainer asked to read the change". The new file declares `Amends:` only on the outage procedure, and its scope there is only who may post. It never amends the acknowledge rule or the Actions-round rule that this clause overrides. Line 29 says a lens's blocking finding stays the maintainer's, but a policy notice comes from a guardrail, not a lens, so that exclusion leaves this hole open. This weakens a fail-closed decision.

properties.failureScenario:
1. A builder's pull request edits `.github/workflows/melian-round.yml`, for example moving `MELIAN_STATUS_TOKEN` into the round job, which runs head code. Or it edits the root `melian.yaml`, for example setting `trust.writers` or lowering a resolution.
2. The `melian round` workflow finishes on the committed routes. Its only finding above advisory is a `policy-change-review` notice. AGENTS.md says such a notice prints as blocking on a workflow or configuration file, so the report job sets `melian/review` to `failure`.
3. CI is green. The coordinator, an agent, reads the diff and the merge base. All four conditions now hold, so it posts `melian/review` `success` under the maintainer's login, with a description ending `; base <sha>`.
4. The merge-group job accepts the status as a writer's status. It is newer than the round's lease-stamped status, so under the coordination decision it outranks it. The job copies it to the group commit, and the change lands.

Wrong outcome: a change to the file that holds the round's logins, or to the policy that decides what blocks, merges without the maintainer reading it and without a stored dismissal. At base that status had to stay `failure` until a host dismissal. The same path works on a pull request the coordinator wrote itself, such as this one, so the agent approves its own policy change.

explanation.whyHere: The point of the policy notice is an independent read by someone who did not write the change. The root-policy floor decision says it exists so a policy edit never lands "with no maintainer asked to read the change". This change is itself an example: a coordinator-authored edit to AGENTS.md's Who does what, which widens the coordinator's powers. AGENTS.md raises a policy notice at acknowledge. Under the new rule, the coordinator's own read of that notice is enough for a builder to queue. The decision's example, pull request #662, shows the builder rightly refused exactly this until now.

properties.failureScenario:
1. The coordinator opens a pull request that edits AGENTS.md's "Who does what" or "Ready and queued", or adds a decision widening its own authority. This pull request is an example: its progress log names the author as "Coordinator."
2. The `melian round` workflow raises a `policy-change-review` notice at acknowledge on AGENTS.md. The status is `success`, as acknowledge does not fail an Actions status.
3. The coordinator reads its own diff and records "Coordinator: read policy notice" on the pull request.
4. By the new line 259 of AGENTS.md, the builder treats that record as the maintainer's read, marks the pull request ready and queues it.

Wrong outcome: a change to the instructions every builder and the coordinator follow, including the trust and queueing rules, lands with its only read made by its own author, an agent posting under the maintainer's login. At base, the actions-round decision and the shards decision required the maintainer's read for every such acknowledge finding except `answers.yaml`.

# What the coordinator may do for the maintainer

Status: ruled by the maintainer on 2026-11-28, in the coordinator's session. The coordinator listed the delegations below, which the maintainer had given one at a time since 2026-10-17, and asked whether to write them into the repository. He answered "yes".

Amends: [When Melian cannot run, the maintainer overrides one commit](2026-10-23-melian-review-outage-procedure.md), who may post the override on a pull request's head: the coordinator too, under the four conditions below

## Problem

The maintainer delegated some of his reads and dismissals to the coordinator, in the coordinator's session. Nothing in the repository said so. A builder cannot check a delegation it cannot read, and all three post under the maintainer's login.

Example: on [pull request #662](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/662), the round's only finding above advisory was a policy notice on one new learning in AGENTS.md. The coordinator read the change and recorded its read. The builder declined to queue on it, rightly, and the pull request waited for the maintainer to answer "read".

## Choice

The coordinator may do these, and nothing else, in the maintainer's place:

1. **Read a policy notice.** The coordinator may read a `policy-change-review` notice on a file whose change it has read, and record that read on the pull request. A builder may queue on that record as it would on the maintainer's.
2. **Dismiss an equivalent mutant**, with a one-line reason that says why no input can tell the mutant from the code.
3. **Dismiss a finding that restates a ruling**: one whose only objection is to a rule the maintainer has ruled on. The dismissal names the ruling's date and where it was given.
4. **Dismiss a refuted injection flag on Melian's own prompt text**: a `melian/injection-attempt` finding the verifier refuted, where the flagged text is Melian's own prompt or its instructions for reviewers, and the coordinator has read the diff of that text and its meaning is unchang [cut at 2 KiB]
